title: Alcohol Allergy: Symptoms, Causes, and Allergy vs Intolerance
excerpt: Is it an alcohol allergy or an intolerance? How to tell them apart, the hidden allergens in beer, wine, and cocktails, sudden reactions, testing, and the signs that need emergency care.
metaDescription: Are you allergic to alcohol or intolerant? Symptoms, hidden allergens in beer and wine, sudden reactions, testing, and anaphylaxis warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a true allergy to alcohol itself (ethanol) is very rare. When people say they're "allergic to alcohol," they almost always mean one of two other things. Either their body breaks alcohol down poorly, which is an intolerance and causes flushing, a stuffy nose, and a fast heartbeat. Or they're reacting to something else in the drink, such as grapes, wheat, barley, yeast, hops, sulfites, histamine, or a fining agent like egg or fish protein. The difference matters because an intolerance is uncomfortable, while a real allergic reaction can turn dangerous within minutes. This guide explains how to tell them apart, which ingredients cause trouble in which drinks, and the signs that mean you need emergency care.

> **When to see a doctor, and when to call 911.** Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away if you or someone with you has **trouble breathing, wheezing, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, a hoarse or tight voice, trouble swallowing, dizziness or fainting, or hives spreading across the body along with vomiting** after a drink. These are signs of anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction. If an epinephrine auto-injector (such as an EpiPen) has been prescribed, use it, then still call 911. Don't wait to see if it settles, and don't assume the person is just very drunk. Book a regular appointment with your doctor or an allergist if you get hives, swelling, wheezing, or stomach cramps after drinking (even mild ones), if reactions are new or getting worse, if you have asthma that flares when you drink, or if you get pain in your lymph nodes (neck, armpit, groin) after alcohol. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Alcohol Allergy vs Alcohol Intolerance: The Key Difference

These two terms get used interchangeably, but they describe different processes in the body.

**An allergy is an immune system reaction.** Your immune system wrongly treats a harmless protein as a threat and makes antibodies (called IgE) against it. The next time you meet that protein, those antibodies tell certain immune cells to release histamine and other chemicals all at once. That's what causes hives, swelling, wheezing, and, in severe cases, a drop in blood pressure. Even a small amount of the trigger can set it off.

**An intolerance is a processing problem.** Your immune system isn't involved. Instead, your body has trouble breaking something down, so it builds up and causes symptoms. The amount matters a lot: a sip might be fine, while a full glass causes trouble.

Here's how they usually compare:

| | Alcohol intolerance | Allergy to something in a drink |
|---|---|---|
| What's going on | Body can't break down alcohol (or histamine) efficiently | Immune system reacts to a specific protein |
| How common | Common, especially in people of East Asian descent | Uncommon |
| Typical symptoms | Facial flushing, warmth, stuffy nose, fast heartbeat, headache, nausea | Hives, itching, swelling, wheezing, stomach cramps, vomiting, dizziness |
| Depends on amount? | Yes, more alcohol usually means worse symptoms | Small amounts can trigger it |
| Every type of drink? | Usually, because ethanol is in all of them | Often only certain drinks (only beer, only red wine, and so on) |
| Can it be dangerous? | Rarely urgent, though it has long-term health implications | Yes, it can cause anaphylaxis |
| Who diagnoses it | Usually recognized from the pattern of symptoms | An allergist, using skin or blood tests |

A useful clue: **if every kind of alcohol does it, intolerance is the likely cause. If only one kind does it, look at the ingredients.** Someone who flushes from beer, wine, and vodka alike probably has trouble processing ethanol. Someone who breaks out in hives only after beer may be reacting to wheat, barley, hops, or yeast.

## Is a True Ethanol Allergy Real?

It exists, but it's rare enough that doctors publish individual cases. A handful of case reports describe people who had hives or anaphylaxis from ethanol itself, sometimes traced to the products the body makes from it, like acetaldehyde and acetic acid, rather than the alcohol molecule. Some of these people also react to alcohol in foods, sauces, and even medicines and mouthwash.

Because it's so rare, an allergist will normally look hard for other explanations first. If you react to many different drinks with true allergy symptoms (hives, swelling, wheezing) rather than flushing, that's exactly the situation where proper testing is worth it.

## Alcohol Intolerance: The Most Common Cause of "Allergy" Symptoms

Most people who think they're allergic to alcohol actually have trouble with the way their body breaks it down.

### How your body processes alcohol

Your liver handles alcohol in two main steps:

1. An enzyme called **alcohol dehydrogenase** turns ethanol into **acetaldehyde**. Acetaldehyde is toxic and causes flushing, a racing heart, nausea, and headache.
2. A second enzyme, **ALDH2 (aldehyde dehydrogenase 2)**, turns acetaldehyde into harmless acetate.

Many people, especially those with East Asian ancestry, carry a gene variant that makes ALDH2 work poorly. Acetaldehyde piles up, and the result is the classic "Asian flush": a red face, neck, and chest, often with a pounding heart and a headache, sometimes after just a few sips. Our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) covers this in depth.

This isn't only a cosmetic issue. Research has linked the ALDH2 variant combined with regular drinking to a higher risk of esophageal cancer, because acetaldehyde is a known carcinogen. If you flush, that's a reason to keep drinking light, not a reason to hide the flush.

### Signs it's an intolerance

- Your face, neck, or chest turns red and warm within minutes
- Your nose gets stuffy or runny
- Your heart beats faster or feels like it's pounding (see our guide to a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking))
- You get a headache or feel nauseous early in the evening
- It happens with every type of alcohol
- It's worse the more you drink

### Sudden alcohol intolerance

If alcohol never bothered you before and now suddenly does, think about what changed. Common reasons include:

- **A new medication.** Some drugs cause a flushing reaction with alcohol because they block the same ALDH2 step. The best-known examples are disulfiram (Antabuse, which is used on purpose for this), the antibiotic metronidazole, and some diabetes and antifungal drugs. Our page on [metronidazole and alcohol](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol) explains this kind of reaction.
- **Hormonal changes**, such as pregnancy or perimenopause.
- **A new allergy**, since allergies can develop in adulthood.
- **Changes in health**, including liver problems.
- **Rarely, a sign of something more serious.** Pain in the lymph nodes after drinking is a recognized, though uncommon, symptom of Hodgkin lymphoma. It's unlikely to be the cause, but new pain like this is worth a doctor's visit.

If a new intolerance appears and you can't explain it, a doctor's appointment is reasonable.

## Alcohol Allergy Symptoms

True allergic reactions to a drink usually start within minutes to about two hours. Symptoms can include:

- **Skin:** hives (raised, itchy welts), itching, redness, swelling of the lips, eyelids, or face
- **Nose and eyes:** sneezing, a runny or blocked nose, itchy watery eyes
- **Breathing:** coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, shortness of breath, or an asthma flare
- **Mouth and throat:** tingling or itching in the mouth, throat tightness, a hoarse voice, trouble swallowing
- **Gut:** stomach cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
- **Circulation:** feeling faint, dizziness, a weak or fast pulse, collapse

The more of these body systems are involved, the more serious the reaction. Hives plus wheezing, or hives plus vomiting and dizziness, is an emergency, not a wait-and-see situation.

One tricky point: being drunk can mask early warning signs. Dizziness, nausea, and a flushed face are easy to blame on the drinks. If someone's lips or tongue are swelling, or they're struggling to breathe, that isn't drunkenness.

## Allergens Hiding in Alcoholic Drinks

Alcoholic drinks are made from plants and processed with a range of helpers. Any of them can be the real culprit. Here's where each one usually shows up.

### Grapes (wine, brandy, some liqueurs)

Grape allergy is uncommon but real. In some people, the trigger is a type of protein called a lipid transfer protein, which is also found in peaches, apples, and other fruits. People with these allergies may react more strongly to wine than to the fruit itself.

### Wheat, barley, rye, and gluten (beer, whisky, some vodkas)

Beer is brewed from malted barley and often wheat, and it keeps a lot of the grain protein. People with a wheat or barley allergy, or with celiac disease (an immune reaction to gluten, which is a different condition from allergy), usually need to avoid regular beer.

Distilled spirits are a different story. Distillation leaves most proteins behind, and celiac organizations such as the Celiac Disease Foundation generally consider pure distilled spirits gluten-free, even when made from wheat or barley. People with a true wheat allergy, though, should talk to their allergist, because tolerance varies and flavored spirits can have ingredients added after distillation.

### Hops (beer)

Allergy to hops is rare, but it's been reported, sometimes in brewery workers. Hoppy styles like IPAs carry more of it.

### Yeast (beer, wine, cider)

Brewer's yeast is used to ferment almost every alcoholic drink. Unfiltered beers and some natural wines carry more of it. A yeast allergy is uncommon but possible.

### Sulfites (wine, cider, some beers)

Sulfites are preservatives that stop wine from spoiling. They're more of a **sensitivity** than a classic allergy, and they mainly affect people with asthma, who may wheeze or cough after sulfite-containing drinks. In the US, any drink with 10 parts per million or more of sulfites must say "contains sulfites" on the label. Contrary to popular belief, white wines often contain as many sulfites as reds, or more. Our guide to [sulfites in wine](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) separates the real effects from the myths.

### Histamine (red wine, aged drinks)

Fermentation creates histamine, the same chemical your body releases in an allergic reaction. Red wine tends to have more than white, and some aged or fermented drinks contain a fair amount. Most people break down dietary histamine easily with an enzyme called DAO (diamine oxidase). Some people have lower DAO activity, and alcohol may interfere with histamine breakdown too. The result can look a lot like an allergy: flushing, headache, a stuffy nose, and itching, without any true immune reaction. This is often called histamine intolerance. Our article on [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) goes through this and the other suspects.

### Fining agents (wine and some beers)

Many wines and some beers are clarified with "fining agents" that bind cloudiness and are then removed. Common ones include egg white (albumin), milk protein (casein), and isinglass (from fish). Tiny traces can remain. In the European Union, wines made with egg or milk products must list them as allergens if they're still detectable. US labels are less consistent, so people with a severe egg, milk, or fish allergy may want to ask the winery or choose wines labeled vegan, which avoid animal-based fining.

### Nuts, fruits, herbs, and other flavorings (liqueurs and mixers)

Liqueurs can contain tree nuts (amaretto, hazelnut and walnut liqueurs), seeds, fruits, herbs, cream, or egg. Cocktails add more possibilities: juices, syrups, dairy, egg white in sours, and garnish. If you have a known food allergy, remember that the cocktail menu is part of the food menu.

### Corn, agave, rice, and other base ingredients

Bourbon and many vodkas are made from corn, tequila from agave, sake from rice, and so on. Allergies to these are uncommon, but they exist.

### Quick reference by drink

| Drink | Possible culprits to consider |
|---|---|
| Beer | Wheat, barley, gluten, hops, yeast, histamine, sometimes sulfites or fining agents |
| Red wine | Grapes, histamine, sulfites, yeast, fining agents (egg, milk, fish) |
| White wine | Grapes, sulfites, yeast, fining agents |
| Cider | Apples, yeast, sulfites |
| Sake | Rice, yeast |
| Clear spirits | Usually few allergens beyond the base ingredient; check flavored versions |
| Liqueurs | Nuts, cream, egg, herbs, fruit, added flavorings |
| Cocktails | Everything in the mixers and garnishes |

## Alcohol Can Make Other Allergies Worse

Even if you're not allergic to anything in your drink, alcohol can change how you react to other allergens.

- **Alcohol is a known "cofactor" for food allergy reactions.** Allergists list alcohol, exercise, certain painkillers, and illness among things that can lower the threshold for a reaction. Someone who normally tolerates a little of a food might react to it after drinking. Alcohol increases gut permeability and widens blood vessels, which may help explain this.
- **It can worsen hay fever and nasal symptoms.** Alcohol widens blood vessels in the nose, and many people notice congestion or sneezing after a drink, especially wine.
- **It can trigger asthma.** Many people with asthma report that some drinks, particularly wine, set off symptoms. Sulfites are one suspect, histamine another.
- **AERD is a special case.** People with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (a condition combining asthma, nasal polyps, and reactions to aspirin and similar painkillers) very often report breathing or nasal symptoms after drinking alcohol. If you have asthma, nasal polyps, and react to alcohol, mention all three to your doctor together.

## How Alcohol Allergy Is Diagnosed

If your symptoms point to a real allergy, an allergist (a doctor who specializes in allergies) can help. A typical approach looks like this:

1. **A detailed history.** Which drinks, how much, how quickly symptoms started, what you ate, and whether exercise or medicines were involved. Keeping notes before your appointment helps a lot.
2. **Skin prick tests.** A tiny amount of a suspected allergen (grape, wheat, yeast, hops, egg, and so on) is placed on your skin to see if it causes a raised bump.
3. **Blood tests.** These measure IgE antibodies to specific allergens.
4. **A supervised challenge.** Sometimes the allergist will have you drink a small, measured amount of the suspected drink in the clinic, where they can treat a reaction immediately. Never try this yourself at home if you've had a serious reaction before.

There's no good evidence that home "food sensitivity" kits that test for IgG antibodies diagnose allergy. Allergy organizations advise against using them for this.

For intolerance caused by ALDH2 deficiency, a formal test usually isn't needed. The flushing pattern itself is the clue, and some people choose genetic testing out of curiosity.

## What to Do If You React to Alcohol

### During a mild reaction

If you only have mild flushing or a stuffy nose and no other symptoms, stop drinking, drink water, and let it settle. Watch for anything spreading or getting worse.

If you get **mild hives or itching only** and no breathing, throat, or dizziness symptoms, stop drinking. Some people take a non-drowsy antihistamine for skin symptoms, but check with a doctor or pharmacist first, because some antihistamines don't mix well with alcohol. Older ones such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl) are sedating, and alcohol makes that drowsiness much stronger. Our guides to [Zyrtec and alcohol](/never-hungover/zyrtec-and-alcohol) and [Benadryl after drinking](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) explain the risks. An antihistamine does not treat anaphylaxis.

### During a severe reaction

Go back to the box at the top: call 911, use epinephrine if it's been prescribed, and have the person lie down with legs raised (or sit up if they're struggling to breathe). Symptoms can return hours later even after they seem to improve, so anyone who needed epinephrine should be checked in an emergency department.

### Afterward

- Write down exactly what you drank, including brand, style, and mixers.
- Avoid that drink until you've seen a doctor.
- Ask whether you need an epinephrine auto-injector and an allergy action plan.
- Tell friends you drink with what to do if it happens again.

## Living With an Alcohol Allergy or Intolerance

### If you have an allergy to a specific ingredient

Avoidance is the main treatment. That means:

- **Read labels and ask.** Check for allergen statements, "contains sulfites," and "vegan" wine labels. Ask bartenders what's in a cocktail.
- **Watch cross-contact.** Shared shakers, jiggers, and garnish trays at bars can carry traces of nuts, dairy, or egg.
- **Carry your epinephrine** if it's been prescribed, and don't let a night out be the time you leave it at home.
- **Be careful with alcohol plus exercise.** Dancing hard after drinks and a meal is exactly the combination that can lower your reaction threshold if you have food allergies.

### If you have intolerance from ALDH2 deficiency

The flush is a signal from your body that acetaldehyde is building up. The safest approach is to drink less or not at all. Some people take acid-reducing antihistamines like famotidine before drinking to hide the redness. That can reduce the visible flush, but it doesn't help clear acetaldehyde, so the toxic build-up continues while the warning sign disappears. Many doctors advise against using them this way.

### If you have histamine or sulfite sensitivity

- Try white wine, or low-histamine options, instead of red, and see if symptoms change
- Clear spirits with simple mixers tend to be the lowest in histamine and sulfites
- Drink slowly and with food
- If you have asthma, keep your reliever inhaler with you and talk to your doctor about wine-triggered symptoms

For a broader comparison of which drinks are easiest on most people, our [least-hangover alcohol ranking](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) is a useful reference, though it's about hangovers, not allergens.

## Can Supplements Help With Alcohol Allergy or Intolerance?

Be cautious here. No supplement treats an allergy, and none should replace avoiding a known trigger or carrying epinephrine.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound that some people take around drinking for hangover support. Lab and animal research suggests it may affect how the body handles alcohol and acetaldehyde, and human data are limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents allergic reactions, fixes ALDH2 deficiency, or reduces the cancer risk linked to flushing. If you simply get ordinary hangovers and have no allergy, it's one option people try; our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how it's typically used, and a widely used product is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), with [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) as a budget option. If you react to drinks with hives, swelling, or wheezing, skip the supplements and see an allergist instead.

**DAO enzyme supplements** are sometimes marketed for histamine intolerance. Evidence is limited, and they don't treat true allergy.

For everyday hangover habits that have the best support, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- A true allergy to ethanol itself is very rare. Most "alcohol allergies" are either an intolerance (trouble breaking alcohol down) or a reaction to another ingredient.
- If every kind of alcohol causes flushing, think intolerance. If one kind causes hives or swelling, think ingredient allergy.
- Common culprits include grapes, wheat, barley, hops, yeast, sulfites, histamine, and fining agents like egg, milk, and fish protein.
- Alcohol can also lower your threshold for reactions to foods and worsen asthma and nasal symptoms.
- Trouble breathing, throat or tongue swelling, or fainting after a drink is an emergency. Use epinephrine if prescribed and call 911.
- An allergist can find the real trigger with skin or blood tests, which beats guessing.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you be allergic to alcohol?**

A true allergy to ethanol itself is very rare, with only scattered case reports. Most people who react to alcohol either have an intolerance, meaning their body can't break alcohol down efficiently, or are allergic or sensitive to another ingredient in the drink, such as grapes, wheat, barley, hops, yeast, sulfites, or fining agents made from egg, milk, or fish.

**What is the difference between an alcohol allergy and alcohol intolerance?**

An allergy is an immune system reaction to a specific protein, and even a small amount can cause hives, swelling, wheezing, or anaphylaxis. An intolerance is a processing problem with no immune involvement, often due to a less active ALDH2 enzyme. It typically causes flushing, a stuffy nose, a fast heartbeat, and headache, and gets worse the more you drink. Intolerance usually happens with all types of alcohol, while allergy is often limited to certain drinks.

**What are the symptoms of an alcohol allergy?**

Symptoms can include hives, itching, swelling of the lips, face, or eyes, a runny or blocked nose, wheezing or chest tightness, tingling in the mouth, stomach cramps, vomiting, and dizziness. They usually start within minutes to about two hours after drinking. Trouble breathing, throat swelling, or fainting are signs of anaphylaxis and need emergency care right away.

**Why do I suddenly get flushed or sick from alcohol?**

New reactions can come from starting a medication that interacts with alcohol (such as metronidazole or disulfiram), hormonal changes like pregnancy or perimenopause, a newly developed allergy to an ingredient, or changes in your health. Rarely, pain in the lymph nodes after drinking can be a sign of Hodgkin lymphoma. If a new reaction appears and you can't explain it, see a doctor.

**Why am I allergic to beer but not wine?**

Beer and wine share very few ingredients besides alcohol and yeast. If you react only to beer, the cause may be wheat, barley, gluten, or hops. If you react only to wine, consider grapes, histamine, sulfites, or fining agents such as egg or milk protein. An allergist can test for these individually.

**Can alcohol cause hives?**

Yes. Hives after drinking can come from an allergy to an ingredient, from histamine in drinks like red wine, or, rarely, from ethanol itself. Alcohol can also make other allergic reactions more likely. Mild hives alone should be checked by a doctor, while hives with breathing trouble, swelling, vomiting, or dizziness need emergency care.

**Can you take an antihistamine before drinking to stop a reaction?**

Ask a doctor first. Antihistamines don't prevent anaphylaxis, and sedating ones such as Benadryl can become dangerously drowsy with alcohol. Using acid-reducing antihistamines to hide Asian flush masks the warning sign without clearing the toxic acetaldehyde that causes it. If you have a true allergy to a drink, avoiding it is the treatment.

**Is there a test for alcohol allergy?**

Yes, for the ingredients. An allergist can run skin prick tests or blood tests for specific allergens such as grape, wheat, barley, yeast, hops, egg, or fish, and may do a supervised drinking challenge in the clinic. Home IgG "food sensitivity" kits are not reliable for diagnosing allergy. Intolerance from ALDH2 deficiency is usually recognized from the flushing pattern alone.
